title: Vedanta (revisited)
hook: the Brahma Sutra opens with "now" and closes by saying the same words twice: no return, no return
tomorrow: each as a lens for a week

segments.voice: Yesterday Vedanta showed its shared shelf: the Upanishads, the Gita, the Brahma Sutra, and every school writing on the same pages. Did you find your idea already in someone else's words? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

The Brahma Sutra ends by saying the same thing twice. After all its packed little lines, the arguments, the objections, the answers, the very last words are: no return, on the word of scripture. No return, on the word of scripture. Tradition reads the doubling as a way of signaling the end, like a bell rung a second time so everyone knows the music is over. We opened this stretch with the book's first word, now. Today we turn to its last. Between them sits the whole book, and with its last line we close our visit to Vedanta.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS TWICE.` → `NO RETURN, NO RETURN.` → `FROM NOW TO THE LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: No return from what? The last part of the Brahma Sutra is about the one who has come to know Brahman, and what happens when this life ends. The answer is that such a one does not come back into the turning of birth and death. And notice what the line rests its case on: the word of scripture. It's leaning on the Chandogya Upanishad, whose closing lines say of the one who reaches the world of Brahman: he does not return, he does not return. The Sutra ends by echoing the Upanishad's own ending. The book that set out to gather the Upanishads finishes in their voice. And then, true to this week, the schools fill in what no return means in their own ways. For Shankara, freedom is knowing what was always so: the self was never anything but Brahman, and nothing needs to travel anywhere. For Ramanuja and for Madhva, the freed self stays itself and lives in the presence of the Lord, whom they know as Vishnu, in a joy that doesn't end. Each reading is argued from these same lines. Now set the first word beside the last. Now: the wish to know. No return: the wish fulfilled. Vedanta, as a darshana, is a way of seeing the whole of life as that kind of journey, from a real question to an answer that doesn't need to be asked again.
screen: `NO RETURN TO BIRTH AND DEATH.` · `ECHOING THE CHANDOGYA'S ENDING.` · `EACH SCHOOL FILLS IN NO RETURN.` · `FROM THE WISH TO THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something be finished. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one small thing that's done, a task, a conversation, a worry that already resolved, and notice how it keeps circling back anyway. Breathe out, and let it not return. Then let it go a second time, gently, the way the Sutra says its last words twice. Rest in whatever is left when that thing stops circling. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Vedanta. From the first word, now, the wish to know, to the last, no return, said twice. Today's word, and the last of our visit with it.
Your line: Vedanta, revisited. Today, when a finished thing comes circling back, say inwardly: done, and done. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Traditional students of the Brahma Sutra read it from its first line to its last, the repeated words 'no return', usually through their own lineage's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's.

original.note: Sanskrit: no return; the Brahma Sutra's last word, said twice.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient book just stops when it runs out.
what it means: the Brahma Sutra ends by saying no return twice, closing the journey that began with the wish to know.
what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 4.4.22, anavrittih shabdat, repeated to mark the end, echoing Chandogya 8.15.1.

sources.ref: Brahma Sutra 4.4.22 (no return, on the authority of scripture; repeated)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.15.1 (he does not return, he does not return)
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on Brahma Sutra 4.4 (the state of the freed self)

notes: Brahma Sutra 4.4.22 anavrittih shabdat anavrittih shabdat: confirm the repetition and the paraphrase 'on the word of scripture'.
'Saying the closing words twice signals the end' is a general claim about Sanskrit texts (repetition marking the close of a chapter or work); confirm or soften to 'tradition reads the repetition as'.
Chandogya 8.15.1 ends na ca punar avartate, na ca punar avartate; confirm the echo.

The schools' accounts of liberation are compressed: Shankara (realizing identity, no going anywhere) versus Ramanuja and Madhva (the freed self in Vishnu's presence, in bliss). Madhva's gradations among the freed are left out. Confirm.
Editor: 'between them sits the whole of Vedanta' narrowed to 'the whole book' (the Brahma Sutra, not the school); the carry is spoken as 'Vedanta, revisited'.
